content: 1. The indicator assesses whether national or subnational standards for social accountability are established and implemented within accreditation mechanisms. It evaluates the inclusion of social accountability in these standards and the involvement of civil society, social stakeholders, and communities in the accreditation process. 2. Social accountability in accreditation mechanisms is defined by the extent to which national or subnational standards reflect this concept. Questions to guide the assessment include whether social accountability is explicitly included in these standards, whether civil society and communities are involved in decision-making, and whether health workforce education institutions measure their impact on the health system and populations they serve. 3. Accreditation mechanisms refer to the systems and processes used to evaluate and ensure the quality of health workforce education and training programs. Accreditation standards are the criteria or benchmarks used to assess these programs, while social accountability refers to the responsibility of institutions to address the health needs of the communities they serve. 4. The indicator on social determinants of health examines whether national or subnational standards include these determinants within accreditation mechanisms. It also evaluates whether health workforce education institutions measure and adapt their curricula to address social determinants of health in the populations they serve. 5. Interprofessional education is assessed by determining whether national or subnational standards include this concept within accreditation mechanisms. Interprofessional education involves training health professionals to work collaboratively across disciplines to improve health outcomes. 6. Cooperation between health workforce education institutions and regulatory bodies is evaluated to determine whether they work together to agree on accreditation standards. This includes assessing the presence of coordinating mechanisms, stakeholder involvement, and institutional systems for negotiating accreditation standards. 7. Continuing professional development (CPD) systems are assessed to determine their existence at national or subnational levels, whether they are mandatory, and if they are linked to relicensure. The integration of CPD into national education plans for the health workforce is also evaluated. 8. In-service training as part of national education plans for the health workforce is assessed to determine its alignment with national health plans and its consideration of policies for transforming professional, technical, and vocational education and training. 9. The module on education finances addresses the funding and investment in health workforce education and training. It tracks expenditures on health workforce education, including pre-service education, and provides information on the cost of health workforce development. 10. Total expenditure on higher education is assessed by examining public and private sources of funding. This includes expenditures on health workforce education, excluding in-service training, and is calculated as a percentage of the gross national income. 11. Average tuition fees per student enrolled in health workforce education and training programs are calculated by dividing the total tuition fees paid by students by the total number of students paying tuition fees. This excludes students exempt from paying tuition. 12. Investment in transformative education and training is assessed by determining whether national health workforce strategies and institutional financing reforms allocate adequate budgetary resources for this purpose. This includes mechanisms to increase sustainable financing for expanding and transforming the health workforce.
